key_insight: The intact brain–skull interface failed within the subarachnoid space and was better represented by a cohesive zone model than by rigid attachment or frictionless sliding with separation.
engineering_relevance: Experimentally identified interface parameters offer more realistic boundary conditions for computational head models.
method: Tested native brain–skull specimens from 19 sheep cadaver heads under tension, compression and shear.
Used histology to verify intact meninges and MRI to build sample-specific finite element models.
Applied inverse finite element analysis to calibrate Ogden brain properties, then cohesive interface parameters.
evidence_signal: Brain shear modulus increased from 0.94 to 1.60 kPa across tested strain rates, while interface peak normal traction (2.35 ± 0.81 kPa), peak tangential traction (4.14 ± 0.97 kPa) and fracture energy (0.35 ± 0.14 N/m) showed no significant rate or loading-mode dependence.
watch_item: Parameters derived from sheep cadaver specimens at the tested rates require validation before use in human head models or higher-rate impact simulations.
paper_title: Mechanical behaviour of the intact brain-skull interface under tension, compression and shear
